method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). We have just seen (while examining Nozick’s account of knowledge) that this requirement is arguably too strong.

But even more importantly, were that a requirement of knowledge (or justification), then we have seen that closure would fail and, consequently, the basis for the first premise in the CP-style argument for Cartesian Skepticism would be forfeited.[12] Ernest Sosa has argued for three interrelated theses regarding CP2
A subjunctive conditional \(A \rightarrow B\) is true if and only if B is true in the closest (or all the closest) possible worlds where A is true.

This means that Sosa cannot accept the possible worlds semantics for subjunctive conditionals briefly sketched above, at least if we assume that every world is closer to itself than any other word.

So far, we have argued that there are dangers in defending CP2 by appealing to the sensitivity condition, and that Sosa’s attack on CP2 might itself be subject to doubt.
Let us take a closer look at the first step, the claim that there is an epistemic symmetry between the good case and the skeptical scenario.
In the good case, for instance, we know mundane propositions such as the proposition that we have hands.
Given CP, in the good case we are justified in believing that we are not in the skeptical case.

For even granting (as we must) that in the skeptical scenario we do not know that we are not in the skeptical scenario, it doesn’t follow that in the ordinary case we do not know that we are not in the skeptical scenario, not even assuming that we have the same evidence in both cases.
Now, the skeptic can then reply that not all skeptical scenarios are such that external worlds propositions are false in them.
Therefore, it can be held that there is an asymmetry between the good case and the skeptical scenario even if we grant that we have the same evidence in both cases.
We noted then that there is at least another possibility: it might be that we must be antecedently justified in believing q in order to be justified in believing some p which entails it.

On one version of this view, put forward by Crispin Wright 2004, our entitlement to accept that we are not in a skeptical scenario does not depend on our having any kind of evidence, either empirical or a priori (see also Coliva 2015 for a development of a view in this neighborhood).
Roughly, what we are calling justification Wright calls “warrant”.

On another version of the view, although we do not have empirical evidence for the proposition that we are not in a skeptical scenario, we do have a kind of justification for it which does not rest exclusively on the fact that if we didn’t then we wouldn’t be justified in believing anything.

Now, we can use that rule “online”, when we do in fact have an experience with the content that there is something red in front of us, or “offline”, assuming for the sake of argument that we have an experience with the content that there is something red in front of us to see what follows from it.
